idiom_name: switch a.(type) { case Circle: switch b.(type) { ... } }
implementation_notes: Go resolves interfaces dynamically but has no method overloading and no inheritance, so the second-dispatch names must encode the receiver type if the interface form is used; the shortest manual form is a nested type switch over (a, b), which reads both dynamic types with language syntax while the pair matrix is still written by hand. Unhandled combinations are runtime panics, and the compiler's exhaustiveness help that closed hierarchies give Java or C# has to be replaced by an explicit default arm - this is why the corpus classes Go as manual rather than idiomatic.
pitfalls: A missing combination is a runtime panic (or a zero value if a default branch returns one): keep the default branch failing loudly.
A type switch sees only the dynamic type, so a pointer receiver (*Circle) and a value receiver (Circle) land in different cases.
Nested switches duplicate the outer cases: extract a type-pair key (a struct of two type descriptors) once the matrix grows.

variants.name: Visitor interface with per-type methods
variants.implementation_notes: The classic structure in Go: a visitor interface whose methods are unique per element type (Go cannot overload, so the receiver type goes into the name) and an Accept(Visitor) method on every element, which gives compile-time breakage across all visitors when an element type is added. The second axis still needs handling - either a visitor type per first-operand type or an assertion inside the method - which is why Go's standard library (go/ast) settles for a single-method Visit plus a type switch inside. Prefer this variant when node types are stable and operations multiply.
pitfalls: Interfaces + methods give coverage over the element axis only; the second axis still needs an assertion or a visitor-per-first-type design.
Adding an element type forces an edit in every visitor implementation, which Go prices as a rebuild of all of them.
A visitor with mutable state is a single-use value in practice: do not reuse it across traversals or goroutines.
